solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Measure across diameter using compasses (5)

indicators.note: to compass is to surround, so WITH closes round D

blocks.note: 'with' = using, as in 'cut with a knife'

annotation.surface: A geometry lesson: measuring a circle across its diameter with a pair of compasses.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Compasses' looks like the drawing instrument that belongs in the scene; here it is a verb meaning encloses, putting D inside WITH.
annotation.definitionFit: Width is a measurement taken across something.

entries.clue: Sinister case of woman developing chill (10)

indicators.note: a case is the outside, so the outer letters of 'woman'
the letters develop into a new form

annotation.surface: Something ominous about a woman's cold getting worse.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Chill' reads as an illness in the surface, but it is the definition: a wintry coldness.
annotation.definitionFit: Wintriness is the quality of being wintry, a chill in the air.

entries.clue: Complete time period, say (3)

blocks.note: to do a job is to complete it

annotation.surface: Talk of a full stretch of time having passed.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Time period' looks like one phrase; split it, and 'period' becomes the punctuation mark. The 'say' tells you a period is only one example of a dot.
annotation.definitionFit: A period, in American usage, is the full stop: a dot.

entries.clue: Awful [in] hospital, but possibly free (6)

blocks.note: h = hospital, as on road signs
'or' offers an alternative, as 'but possibly' does
to rid is to free (of something)

annotation.surface: A grim hospital stay, though at least treatment might be free.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface nods at a free health service; 'free' is really the verb, as in ridding yourself of something.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both describe something very unpleasant.

entries.clue: Rat with cat coming over is first to disappear (2,7)

indicators.note: the word turns over, so MOG reads backwards
GOM goes in front of the rest

blocks.note: a mog is a cat; reversed to GOM
to rat on someone is to sing, to inform

annotation.surface: A cat and rat together, the rat taking care to vanish first.
annotation.walkthrough: Rat and cat look like two animals; 'Rat' is the verb, to inform on, which is to sing. MOG is British slang for a cat.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: things that go missing have vanished, the phrasal equivalent of the single verb.

entries.clue: Illegal act I condemn involves kicking superstar (9)

indicators.note: the phrase contains the answer inside it

annotation.surface: Someone condemning an illegal act of kicking a star.
annotation.walkthrough: A galactico is a star footballer, from Real Madrid's big-money signings; 'kicking' makes the definition a football player rather than an assault.
annotation.definitionFit: A galactico is a superstar footballer, a star who kicks a ball.

entries.clue: Local chief agreed men should have married first (5)

indicators.note: M is placed at the front of the answer

blocks.note: OR = other ranks, soldiers who are not officers

annotation.surface: A local leader insisting men should have been married before anything else.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface sounds like a small-town rule on marriage; 'men' is the army's other ranks.
annotation.definitionFit: A mayor is the chief civic officer of a town.

entries.clue: Break down resistance [of] son frequently in court (6,2)

blocks.note: to be up before the judge is to be in court

annotation.surface: A father despairing of a son who keeps ending up in court.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Up' for 'in court' is a British idiom: someone 'up before the magistrates' is appearing in court.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom from boxing and persuasion: you weaken an opponent's resistance before the real attack or request.

entries.clue: Under canvas, you’d say one’s not on it? (11)

indicators.note: tells you to go by the sound when spoken

blocks.note: under canvas = in a tent; one's = one has = I've

annotation.surface: A camper, asked where something is, replying that it isn't there.
annotation.walkthrough: 'One's' must be read as 'one has', which gives I'VE; spoken quickly, 'in a tent I've' is inattentive.
annotation.definitionFit: A slangy definition: being 'on it' means alert and switched on, so not on it is its opposite.

entries.clue: Bind grating that’s twisted in the middle (4)

indicators.note: something twisted is turned round on itself, so those letters face the other way
only the central letters RI are turned

blocks.note: a grid is a grating; its middle RI turns to IR

annotation.surface: Tying up a metal grating that has buckled in the centre.
annotation.walkthrough: Only the two middle letters of GRID swap round, leaving G and D in place.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in an old-fashioned register: girding a sword on means binding it round the waist.

entries.clue: Of course you recover after turning brown (9)

indicators.note: U RALLY comes after the turned word
a word that turns round faces the other way, so TAN reads backwards

blocks.note: tan is a brown; reversed to NAT

annotation.surface: Reassurance that you'll recover once you've gone brown in the sun.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface reads like advice after sunburn; 'turning brown' is really TAN turned round.
annotation.definitionFit: Naturally and of course both mean 'as expected'.

entries.clue: Sudden blaze reported [in] particular faculty (5)

indicators.note: tells you to go by the sound when spoken

blocks.note: a flare is a sudden blaze of light

annotation.surface: A news item about a sudden fire at a university department.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Faculty' suggests a university department; here it is a natural ability.
annotation.definitionFit: A flair is a special aptitude, a particular faculty for something.

entries.clue: Funny wee fellow turning ten in October has run ahead (6,7)

indicators.note: the letters turn into a new order
to be ahead is to be in front, so R leads the anagrammed letters

annotation.surface: A little boy turning ten in October who races ahead of everyone.
annotation.walkthrough: Ronnie Corbett was a very short British comedian, one of The Two Ronnies; the surface's birthday boy is really the fodder 'ten in October'.
annotation.definitionFit: Ronnie Corbett was a comedian famous for being small: a funny wee fellow.

entries.clue: Forecaster covering crazy techniques up with common sense (11)

indicators.note: NOUS wraps round the other letters
in a down clue, the letters read upwards, i.e. backwards

blocks.note: nous = common sense; it goes round STRADAM

annotation.surface: A forecaster hiding mad methods behind a show of good sense.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Up' is a reversal only because this is a down clue; common sense as NOUS is a British informal word worth knowing.
annotation.definitionFit: Nostradamus was the famous 16th-century French prophet.

entries.clue: Notice a homo sapiens evolves, losing half its ancestry? (4,3,3)

indicators.note: DEVELOPS drops its second half, LOPS

blocks.note: DEVELOPS with half its letters gone

annotation.surface: A remark that humanity's evolution has cost it half its family tree.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Its' points back to homo sapiens, so the definition is man's ancestry in the Biblical account; the question mark admits the stretch.
annotation.definitionFit: In Genesis, Adam and Eve are the first ancestors of all humankind.

entries.clue: Eat seconds of infected food and keep it down (4)

indicators.note: take the second letter of each word

blocks.note: sh! = keep it down, be quiet

annotation.surface: Going back for more of a dodgy dish and trying not to be sick.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Seconds' and 'keep it down' both read as eating in the surface; one picks second letters, the other means be quiet. Nosh is British slang for food or eating.
annotation.definitionFit: A regional use: British slang for eating, as in having a nosh-up.

entries.clue: Dud brew inn concocted, considerably overblown? (10)

indicators.note: the letters are mixed up into something new

annotation.surface: A pub brewing duff beer and making great claims for it.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Overblown' seems to mean exaggerated, but read literally it is having had too much wind blown over you, which chaps the skin.
annotation.definitionFit: Skin that has been blown over by wind a great deal becomes windburned.

entries.clue: Career over, walk [in] remote regions (4,5)

indicators.note: in a down clue the word turns over, reading backwards

blocks.note: to career is to speed along

annotation.surface: Someone whose career is over taking long walks in faraway places.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Career over' reads as retirement; 'career' is the verb to rush, so SPEED turns over.
annotation.definitionFit: Deep space is the remote region beyond the solar system.

entries.clue: Stretch tallest man on board [for] punishment (8)

blocks.note: a span is a stretch of time or distance
the king is the tallest chess piece

annotation.surface: The tallest man on a company board is stretched on the rack as punishment.
annotation.walkthrough: 'On board' means on a chessboard, where the king is the tallest piece, not a company board.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a smacked bottom is one form of punishment, chiefly for children.

entries.clue: Keep gambling habit on winning this? (5,5)

annotation.definition: Keep gambling habit on winning this?

blocks.note: the surface reading: sustaining an addiction to betting; really 'keep habit on', a habit being a garment
the game where winning is the only way to stay dressed

annotation.surface: Advice on sustaining a gambling addiction by winning.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Habit' reads as an addiction; it is clothing, as a nun wears. In strip poker losers shed clothes, so only by winning do you keep your habit on.
annotation.definitionFit: In strip poker the losers remove clothing, so winners keep theirs on.

entries.clue: Partners’ concern [when] video changes hands? (4)

indicators.note: L (left) is swapped for R (right)

blocks.note: a video is a film; its L becomes R

annotation.surface: A partnership worried about who now owns a video.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Concern' means business, and 'changes hands' is left to right, L to R.
annotation.definitionFit: A firm is a business concern, often run by partners.

entries.clue: Bar closing for April, stagger home — poor kid (6)

indicators.note: to bar is to exclude, so a letter is removed
points to the last letter of April, L

blocks.note: the L at the end of APRIL is excluded
to lurch is to stagger; it loses its L to leave URCH

annotation.surface: A pub shutting in April and a drunk staggering home past a ragged child.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bar' is not a pub but the verb to exclude, and 'closing for April' is its last letter, L.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym with a dated flavour: a street child in rags, the Artful Dodger type.

entries.clue: National Theatre distributes egg sandwiches, one nearly filling expert? (6,7)

indicators.note: DEALS URGE goes either side of NT
ONE loses its last letter

blocks.note: to egg on is to urge
the NT, London's National Theatre, sits inside DEALSURGE

annotation.surface: The National Theatre café handing out egg sandwiches, one almost overflowing.
annotation.walkthrough: The food picture makes 'egg' a noun and 'filling' a sandwich filling; egg is the verb urge, and the filling goes in a tooth.
annotation.definitionFit: A cryptic definition: 'filling' suggests a sandwich, but the expert fills teeth.

entries.clue: Courts cutting a hearing short (5)

indicators.note: the word is cut short, losing its last letter

blocks.note: TRIAL, a court hearing, without its last letter

annotation.surface: Law courts truncating a hearing.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Courts' suggests law courts; the definition means courtyards, the open central spaces of Roman houses.
annotation.definitionFit: Atria are open central courts in buildings, plural of atrium.

entries.clue: Fast cloud [in which] odd bits of ash could drop (4)

indicators.note: points to the odd-numbered letters
those odd letters are dropped, leaving the even ones

blocks.clueFragment: odd bits of ash could drop
blocks.note: a S h C o U l D: drop the odd letters

annotation.surface: A cloud blowing past a volcano, scattering ash.
annotation.walkthrough: The trap is taking the odd letters (AHOL); 'drop' says they are thrown away, leaving the even ones.
annotation.definitionFit: Scud is low, ragged cloud driven fast by the wind.

entries.clue: Implement for easing locks one used for different purposes (5)

annotation.surface: A burglar's tool for opening locks, with several uses.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Locks' suggests doors and burglars; they are locks of hair. A combi is a British term for a multi-purpose appliance, like a combi boiler.
annotation.definitionFit: Combi describes something combining several functions, used for different purposes.

entries.clue: Henry half-way along on a rope within touching distance (9)

indicators.note: H is placed partway through A CABLE

blocks.note: a cable is a heavy rope; H goes in its middle
h = henry, the unit of inductance

annotation.surface: A man called Henry halfway along a rope, nearly within reach.
annotation.walkthrough: Henry looks like a name; it is the physics unit, symbol H.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both describe being close enough to touch.

entries.clue: Tape with name cut off (3)

indicators.note: a cut removes something, here the letter for name

blocks.note: a band is a strip, a tape

annotation.surface: Cutting a label with a name off a tape.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cut off' looks like one phrasal verb; 'cut' works on the name and 'off' is the definition, as food goes off.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the food sense: milk that has turned is spoiled.

entries.clue: Authentically Asian spiciness reflected eastern style (9)

indicators.note: a reflection runs the word backwards

blocks.note: a tang is a sharp flavour; reversed to GNAT

annotation.surface: A curry described as genuinely Asian, its spice echoing an eastern style.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Style' reads as a cooking style but is the verb, to call by a title. Desi, from Hindi, is common in British usage for South Asian things.
annotation.definitionFit: To style someone something is to name them that, to designate them.

entries.clue: Encouragement for one horse coming from the rear (5)

indicators.note: the letters read from the back, reversed

blocks.note: a dun is a greyish-brown horse

annotation.surface: Urging a horse on from behind.
annotation.walkthrough: 'For one' gives EG, for example, and a dun is a horse of dull brown colour.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a gentle push towards doing something is a mild form of encouragement.
